title: Nipah Virus: Human Immune Responses, Transmission Mechanisms, and Vaccine Development
abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a zoonotic paramyxovirus that causes severe disease in humans, characterized by encephalitis and respiratory symptoms with high mortality. First identified in a 1998–99 outbreak in Malaysia, NiV has since caused sporadic outbreaks in South Asia with case fatality rates ranging from ~40% to 75%. Human infection typically results from spillover of the virus from its natural reservoir, fruit bats of the Pteropus genus. Human-to-human transmission can occur, especially with the NiV-Bangladesh strain, raising pandemic concerns despite NiV’s limited sustained transmissibility. This systematic review examines the human immunological response to NiV infection and its interplay with pathogenesis, discusses the mechanisms of NiV transmission from bats to humans and among humans, and reviews the current landscape of NiV vaccine development. NiV has evolved multiple strategies to evade innate immunity, and an effective immune response (involving both robust interferon activity and adaptive responses) is critical for host survival. Major transmission pathways include bat-to-human (e.g. via contaminated date palm sap), animal-to-human (e.g. via pigs or horses), and close-contact spread, which have been implicated in several outbreaks. Finally, I summarize progress in NiV vaccine research: several vaccine candidates (e.g., viral-vectored, subunit, and mRNA-based vaccines) have demonstrated protective immunity in preclinical models and are in Phase 1 trials. Given the rarity of outbreaks, innovative regulatory strategies are being pursued to expedite vaccine availability. Overall, strengthening our understanding of NiV immunity and transmission, alongside advancing vaccines, is pivotal to reduce the threat of this deadly virus.

analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that further research is needed to better understand NiV immunity and transmission dynamics. abstract_zh: 尼帕病毒 (NiV) 是一种人畜共患副粘病毒,可导致人类严重疾病,其特征为 脑炎 和高 死亡率 的呼吸道症状。NiV 于 1998-99 年在马来西亚的 暴发 中首次被发现,此后在南亚引起了零星的 暴发,病死率约为 40% 至 75%。人类感染通常由来自翼龙属的天然 储存宿主、果蝠 病毒的 跨物种溢出 引起。人与人之间的 传播 可能会发生,尤其是 NiV-孟加拉国毒株,尽管 NiV 的持续传播能力有限,但仍引起了大流行的担忧。这篇系统综述研究了人类对 NiV 感染的免疫反应及其与 发病机制 的相互作用,讨论了 NiV 传播 从蝙蝠到人类以及人类之间的机制,并回顾了 NiV 疫苗 发展的现状。NiV 已经进化出多种策略来逃避先天免疫,而有效的 免疫应答(涉及强大的干扰素活性和适应性反应)对于 宿主 的生存至关重要。传播 的主要传播途径包括蝙蝠传人(例如通过受污染的枣椰汁)、动物传人(例如通过猪或马)以及近距离接触传播,这些途径与多个 暴发 病毒有关。最后,我总结了 NiV 疫苗 研究的进展:几种 疫苗 候选药物(例如,病毒载体、亚基和基于 mRNA 的 疫苗)已在临床前模型中证明了保护性免疫,并且正在进行 1 期试验。鉴于 暴发 的稀有性,我们正在寻求创新的监管策略来加快 疫苗 的可用性。总体而言,加强我们对 NiV 免疫和 传播 的理解,同时推进 疫苗,对于减少这种致命病毒的威胁至关重要。

title: Countering Nipah Virus: A Review of Pathogenesis, Countermeasure Design, and Biosecurity Challenges
abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a zoonotic pathogen classified by the World Health Organization as a priority pathogen with epidemic potential.Driven by distinct viral lineages in Malaysia and Bangladesh, this pathogen can induce severe respiratory illness and lethal encephalitis, with human mortality rates ranging from ~40% to ~75% across outbreak zones, depending on the strain.This review paper focuses on the zoonotic origins and molecular mechanisms underlying NiV infection while highlighting both current medical countermeasures and emerging translational avenues to counter NiV's capacity for host immune evasion.By mapping out how these novel therapeutic strategies target the host-pathogen interface, we aim to inspire future countermeasure development and improve clinical outcomes for this biosecurity-relevant disease. Overview of Nipah VirusNipah virus (NiV) is an extremely pathogenic, zoonotic, single stranded RNA virus.Zoonotic viruses are viruses commonly transmitted to humans through animals.The pathogen exists in an animal reservoir where it can stay without dying out, eventually spreading to humans through infected animals or contaminated materials like food or fluids.Nipah virus is part of the family Paramyxoviridae, which is a family of enveloped, non-segmented, negative sense single stranded RNA viruses (Madhukalya et al., 2025).Members of the family will usually infect many mammals and birds, causing damage to the respiratory and nervous system.Viruses of the Paramyxoviridae family can range from common viruses like the measles virus and mumps virus all the way to lethal viruses such as Nipah virus (Madhukalya et al., 2025).Within that family, Nipah virus belongs to genus Henipavirus, a smaller group within the family that shares more commonalities.Members of genus Henipavirus tend to infect several different mammal species, are highly pathogenic, and can harbor a large number of hosts (Madhukalya et al., 2025).The most common hosts for viruses in this genus are fruit bats of genus Pteropus (Madhukalya et al., 2025).Hendra virus, a member of genus Henipavirus, is the closest relative to Nipah virus, and shares many commonalities, such as the same host and similar tissue tropism (Madhukalya et al., 2025).These similarities have led to attempts to utilize studies on Hendra in regards to finding antivirals and treatments for Nipah virus.Nipah virus contains a single stranded RNA genome, meaning genetic material is stored in RNA rather than DNA (Pellett et al., 2014).Single stranded means that the virus consists of only one RNA strand as opposed to the complementary strands of DNA (Pellett et al., 2014).However, this single strand means that Nipah, along with other RNA viruses, can mutate very fast, as RNA replication tends to be less accurate than DNA replication, allowing for more mutations to survive the replication process and pass their traits down (Madhukalya et al., 2025).In addition to being single stranded, Nipah virus is also negative-sense.This means that the virus cannot be used immediately to make proteins with the cell's organelles (Madhukalya et al., 2025).The RNA genetic sequence is already complementary to typical mRNA that can be translated into protein, so the virus must make a positive sense strand of RNA before protein production can begin (Pellett et al., 2014).This is done with RNA-dependent RNA polymerase

elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 尼帕病毒 (NiV) 是一种人畜共患病原体,被世界卫生组织列为具有流行潜力的优先病原体。在马来西亚和孟加拉国独特的病毒谱系驱动下,这种病原体可诱发严重呼吸道疾病和致命的 脑炎,根据菌株的不同,在 死亡率 区域,人类 死亡率 发病率范围为 ~40% 至 ~75%。这篇综述论文重点介绍了人畜共患起源和潜在的分子机制NiV 感染,同时强调当前的医疗对策和新兴的转化途径,以对抗 NiV 宿主 免疫逃避的能力。通过规划这些新颖的治疗策略如何针对 宿主 病原体界面,我们的目标是激发未来的对策开发并改善这种生物安全相关疾病的临床结果。

title: Understanding Wildlife–Livestock–Human Interface for Prevention and Control of Emerging and Re-Emerging Infectious Diseases
abstract: Emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases (EIDs and REIDs) continue to pose a major threat to human and animal health globally. The close interactions among wildlife, livestock, and humans especially in areas where natural habitats are disturbed create ideal conditions for diseases to spill over from animals to humans. Changes in land use, deforestation, climate change, urban expansion, and global travel have contributed both to the rise in new infections and the return of old ones. Outbreaks of Nipah virus in Malaysia, Ebola in West Africa, and COVID-19 highlight the large-scale epidemics caused by human–wildlife contact. Ecological pressure and increasing movement of people and goods have facilitated the cross-species transmission of pathogens. In India, outbreaks of diseases like Lumpy Skin Disease, avian influenza, and Nipah virus have affected both public health and the livestock sector, causing significant economic losses. The One Health approach—linking human, animal, and environmental health—is now essential for controlling disease risk. Strategies like improved surveillance, better diagnostics, vaccine development, responsible use of antibiotics, and restoration of ecological buffer zones are essential in mitigating the risk of disease. This review emphasizes the need for coordinated action across disciplines to reduce future outbreaks and improve preparedness for zoonotic and environmentally driven infectious diseases.

The review underscores the importance of the One Health approach in managing disease risks and calls for improved surveillance, diagnostics, and vaccine development. The findings emphasize the need for coordinated action across disciplines to reduce future outbreaks and enhance preparedness for zoonotic diseases.

elements_en.scope_and_question: The review focuses on Nipah virus (Henipavirus nipahense), Nipah virus infection, and Nipah virus disease. It examines the role of the wildlife–livestock–human interface in the emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases, with a specific emphasis on Nipah virus and its associated health impacts.
elements_en.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a systematic analysis of the literature on Nipah virus and related factors. It includes studies on ecological pressures, land use changes, and cross-species transmission. The review does not explicitly report on meta-analysis or consensus processes, but it synthesizes findings from multiple sources to highlight the importance of the wildlife–livestock–human interface in disease dynamics.
elements_en.consensus_and_key_conclusions: There is a consensus that Nipah virus outbreaks are linked to human–wildlife interactions, particularly in areas with disturbed natural habitats. The review concludes that ecological changes and increased human movement have facilitated the cross-species transmission of pathogens, including Nipah virus, and that the One Health approach is essential for managing these risks.
elements_en.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies gaps in understanding the specific mechanisms of Nipah virus transmission and the role of different animal species as reservoirs. There is also a lack of comprehensive data on the long-term effects of Nipah virus outbreaks on both human and animal populations.
elements_en.research_and_practice_implications: The review highlights the need for improved surveillance, better diagnostics, and vaccine development to mitigate the risk of Nipah virus outbreaks. It also emphasizes the importance of restoring ecological buffer zones and implementing responsible antibiotic use to reduce future disease transmission events.

title_zh: 了解野生动物-牲畜-人类之间的相互作用以预防和控制新发和再发传染病
source_body_en: Emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases (EIDs and REIDs) continue to pose a major threat to human and animal health globally. The close interactions among wildlife, livestock, and humans especially in areas where natural habitats are disturbed create ideal conditions for diseases to spill over from animals to humans. Changes in land use, deforestation, climate change, urban expansion, and global travel have contributed both to the rise in new infections and the return of old ones. Outbreaks of Nipah virus in Malaysia, Ebola in West Africa, and COVID-19 highlight the large-scale epidemics caused by human–wildlife contact. Ecological pressure and increasing movement of people and goods have facilitated the cross-species transmission of pathogens. In India, outbreaks of diseases like Lumpy Skin Disease, avian influenza, and Nipah virus have affected both public health and the livestock sector, causing significant economic losses. The One Health approach—linking human, animal, and environmental health—is now essential for controlling disease risk. Strategies like improved surveillance, better diagnostics, vaccine development, responsible use of antibiotics, and restoration of ecological buffer zones are essential in mitigating the risk of disease. This review emphasizes the need for coordinated action across disciplines to reduce future outbreaks and improve preparedness for zoonotic and environmentally driven infectious diseases.

title: Hemagglutinin and fusion proteins precede measles virus ribonucleoproteins and marshal cell-to-cell spread in airway epithelium.
abstract: ABSTRACT Measles virus (MeV) is the most contagious human respiratory pathogen. To understand how it spreads in the airways, we infected well-differentiated primary cultures of human airway epithelial cells (HAE). We discovered that the MeV attachment protein (hemagglutinin, H), the fusion (F) protein, and the assembly organizer protein (matrix, M) reach newly infected cells ahead of, and independently from, the replicative complex proteins. To characterize the mechanisms of MeV spread, we generated a replication-deficient adenoviral vector expressing the MeV M, F, and H proteins in a doxycycline-inducible manner. This viral vector formed infectious centers that preserved epithelial function like those from MeV infection. To further dissect this process, we generated Ad vectors expressing individual MeV proteins, termed Ad-M, Ad-F, and Ad-H. Transduction of HAE with single, double, and triple Ad vector combinations revealed that Ad-F and Ad-H are necessary and sufficient to form MeV-like infectious centers. MeV enters and spreads within airway epithelia via H protein binding to adherens junction protein, nectin-4. To disrupt spread, we introduced the point mutation HY543A, a mutation previously described to inhibit nectin-4 binding, in the Ad-H vector. Co-transduction of Ad-F and Ad-HY543A did not result in MeV-like infectious center formation. Finally, we assessed whether the MeV-related paramyxovirus Nipah (NiV) attachment and fusion proteins (G and F, respectively) support cell-to-cell spread. Co-transduction of HAE with Ad-NiV-G and Ad-NiV-F did not result in infectious center formation, suggesting that decoupling of the membrane fusion apparatus function from replication is a unique feature of the MeV envelope glycoproteins. IMPORTANCE Measles virus is a highly contagious pathogen. We characterized a mechanism by which measles virus spreads rapidly through the cells that line the human airway in an ex vivo model. We show that the proteins of the viral membrane fusion apparatus, hemagglutinin (H) and fusion (F), move independently from and reach newly infected cells before the proteins of the replicative complex. Thus, viral protein spread is assembled and arranged in order (i.e., marshaled). Using adenovirus-based vectors, we show that co-expression of H and F proteins promotes rapid sequential spread to multiple cells and the formation of infectious centers. Further elucidation of the mechanism of measles virus amplification and cell-to-cell spread within the lung may help explain its highly contagious nature. Measles virus is a highly contagious pathogen.

title: Interpreting changes in reported case fatality in endemic zoonoses: an analytical framework and ecological analysis of Lassa fever surveillance in Nigeria, 2017-26
abstract: BackgroundNigerias reported Lassa fever case fatality ratio (CFR) rose from 18.9% at week 23 of 2025 to 25.0% in 2026, prompting concerns over failing clinical care. Because surveillance artefacts can also alter CFRs, candidate mechanisms that published data can resolve were identified and evaluated. MethodsThis ecological study extracted weekly state-level counts from 474 Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention situation reports (2017-2026). Per a pre-specified plan, years were compared at phase-matched points, year-on-year CFR changes were decomposed into within-state and between-state components, and tipping-point ascertainment shifts calculated. analysis_zh.methods: 从 474 份情况报告中提取了每周事件和累积病例数。使用预先指定的计划来比较各个阶段的阶段匹配点,将同比 CFR 变化分解为州内和州间组成部分,并计算临界点确定偏移。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,2026 年病死率的上升是由于每周计数之外的累计死亡人数增加,而不是由于临床护理的变化。本研究引入了一个框架,用于解释报告的复发性 跨物种溢出 人畜共患病 CFR 的变化。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,如果没有关于检测量、后期死亡人数和尸检采样的额外信息,已发布的地方性人畜共患病 CFR 数据不能用作可靠的临床结果衡量标准。这对于跟踪国家 CFR 目标的进展和规划 疫苗 试验具有影响。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的证据强度中等,因为可以单独解释 CFR 变化的数据(例如检测的标本和后期添加的死亡)已收集但未发表。这限制了充分评估研究结果有效性的能力。

full_text: IntroductionZoonotic disease outbreaks are increasing in frequency and complexity, highlighting the need for intelligent surveillance systems capable of real-time monitoring and risk assessment. Existing surveillance approaches are often reactive, fragmented, and dependent on manual analysis, limiting timely public health responses.MethodsThis study presents TransmiRisk-AI, an agentic AI-driven surveillance framework designed to support automated zoonotic disease risk monitoring and decision-making. The framework integrates a hybrid risk scoring model with a multi-agent architecture comprising data ingestion, risk assessment, alert generation, execution, logging, and orchestration agents. These agents collaboratively automate data collection, preprocessing, risk evaluation, outbreak monitoring, and alert dissemination. To enhance situational awareness, the system incorporates outbreak intelligence from WHO Disease Outbreak News and dynamically updates disease risk profiles based on outbreak recency, frequency, and severity. An interactive Streamlit dashboard provides transparent visualization of risk categories, outbreak trends, and system activities.ResultsCase studies involving the Nipah virus and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever demonstrate the framework's ability to adapt to evolving epidemiological conditions.DiscussionTransmiRisk-AI offers a scalable and interpretable digital health solution that supports proactive surveillance and timely decision-making within a One Health context. 3MethodologyThe TransmiRisk-AI conceptualization is an autonomous, goal-oriented framework of surveillance based on a multi-agent structure. The system allows the active consumption of heterogeneous data streams, real-time risk assessment, and instantaneous alerts to be issued due to the integrated communication between specialized agents. It has a modular and scalable architecture that enables execution of tasks independently and ensures overall system coherence through centralized orchestration.3.1Data sources and input preparation3.1.1Structured zoonotic disease datasetThe TransmiRisk-AI architecture makes use of a pre-constructed structured dataset for zoonotic diseases as the knowledge base for autonomous risk evaluation. There are 124 zoonotic diseases, including viral, bacterial, parasitic and fungal pathogens relevant to global public health surveillance. The data set was compiled from World Health Organization, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, other published and scientificly valid sources. The construction of the original dataset and the hybrid scoring approach has been used in the previous TransmiRisk framework.The epidemiological and ecological attributes of each disease are provided in a structured format that is essential for automated risk computation, and comprise: Transmission characteristicsHost species and zoonotic interface.Clinical severity indicatorsHigh-risk human populationsEnvironmental exposure conditionsComplexity of treatment and diagnosisThese structured attributes allow the implementation of rules for scoring and for downstream risk assessment by the agents.3.1.2Ecological spillover data integrationThe virus level spillover scores were combined with the EcoHealth Alliance SpillOver dataset to capture potential of ecological emergence. Zoonotic viruses were mapped to the diseases in the master dataset based on the standardized disease–virus matching. The spillover scores were then normed and fed into the agentic scoring engine as ecological risk inputs.3.1.3Real-time outbreak intelligenceTo support dynamic surveillance, outbreak information was collected from the World Health Organization. Outbreak reports are continuously monitored and outbreak indicators such as: The number of confirmed cases are reported.Number of cases confirmed.Number of deathsRecentness of outbreak eventsThese real-time signals are fed into the ingestion agent to be processed and applied for dynamic risk recalculation in the TransmiRisk-AI framework.Role of Historical Disease Data: Transmission history of zoonotic diseases can be used as a knowledge base in structured form, which is useful for comparative risk assessment. The format allows the dataset to be used to represent a variety of diseases with a common set of epidemiological, clinical, transmission, ecological and risk attributes so that the framework can be used to identify and compare disease risk attributes. The Rule-based and Hybrid scoring components have as their input basis these historical records. The system doesn’t automatically retrain or adjust the underlying scoring rules when it receives newly observed outbreak signals, instead, the newly observed outbreak signals are added onto the outbreak component to dynamically update the composite risk assessment. The machine-learning part utilizes past disease data for training purposes. The features selected are then fed to the learning algorithm along with the risk labels, so that the learning algorithm can learn statistical associations between disease features and risk categories. The trained model then can be used to classify new records according to these relationships. This is learning, apart from the rule-based composite risk calculation and the autonomous agent orchestration.3.2Overview of TransmiRisk-AI systemTransmiRisk-AI builds on the previously developed TransmiRisk framework by the authors (45). The previous one set a framework for a rule-based epidemiological risk assessment approach for zoonotic diseases. In this study, this component of the risk assessment remains and is combined with information on ecological spillover and real-time outbreak intelligence to create a hybrid layer of risk assessment. This hybrid layer is then integrated into a multi-agent architecture to allow for automated data ingestion, risk recalculation, alert generation, logging and workflow orchestration.The TransmiRisk-AI system comprises of six main agents, including Data Ingest Agent, Risk Evaluation Agent, Action Execution Agent, Alert Agent, Logger Agent and an Orchestrator. These agents work together in a sequence and event-based workflow to complete end-to-end surveillance tasks. The system combines a variety of data sources, such as structured datasets of zoonotic data and real-time information on outbreaks to derive continuously updated risk estimates.The architecture supports both periodic execution and on-demand execution, allowing periodic monitoring and responsiveness to new data in real-time. Individual agents are supposed to do a given job and this is why they are modular, fault tolerant, and extensible.3.3Multi-agent workflowFigure 1 shows the general structure of the TransmiRisk-AI system. The TransmiRisk-AI workflow starts with data ingestion, whereby new datasets or updates on outbreaks are identified and processed by the Data Ingest Agent. The processed data is then sent to the Risk Evaluation Agent where new risk scores of all the diseases are calculated. These results are then stored in the Action Execution Agent and produce structured outputs.Figure 1TransmiRisk agentic-AI workflow.Flowchart illustrating an outbreak risk evaluation framework with five main agents: data ingest, risk evaluation, risk change detection, alert, and action execution, supported by input sources, trigger modes, system support, and outputs including updated datasets, event logs, dashboards, and heatmaps. Color-coded legend indicates each agent’s function.After risk computation, the Alert Agent assesses the results and in case of critical events produces alerts where needed. At the same time, the Logger Agent logs all the actions and decisions during the workflow. This whole process is coordinated by the Orchestrator who makes sure that there is a smooth flow.This pipeline also allows running batch and real-time monitoring and thus the system can dynamically change as new data sources are added and the conditions of outbreaks change.The architecture emphasizes the modularity of the system, with every agent undertaking a specific task, but playing a role in the final goal of autonomous and real-time zoonotic risk surveillance. This architecture improves scalability, flexibility, and robustness and the framework can be deployed to dynamic public health settings.3.4Agents and their rolesThe TransmiRisk-AI framework is composed of multiple specialized agents, each responsible for a specific task within the risk assessment pipeline, as summarized in Table 1.Table 1Agent definitions and functional roles in TransmiRisk-AI.Agent nameRoleFunction descriptionData ingestion agentData CollectionCollects and preprocesses multi-source data including epidemiological, ecological, and outbreak datasetsRisk evaluation agentRisk ComputationComputes composite risk scores using hybrid modeling and predefined thresholdsAction execution agentDecision ImplementationExecutes system actions such as triggering workflows, updating dashboards, or initiating interventionsAlert agentNotificationGenerates real-time alerts for high-risk scenarios and abnormal patternsLogger agentMonitoring &LoggingRecords system activities, agent decisions, and execution logs for traceability and auditingOrchestrator agentCoordinationManages communication and workflow between agents to ensure seamless execution3.5Agent descriptions3.5.1Data ingest agentWe have developed an automatic data preprocessing and integration pipeline to ensure quality, consistency and usability of multi-source zoonotic data. The pipeline will be constantly monitoring a given input folder for new datasets when they are uploaded. If the system detects new datasets, it automatically invokes a series of validations and pre-processing.The new dataset (Dnew) is first loaded and schema validation is performed, which consists of verifying the existence of the necessary attributes and the compliance of the data types. Data which does not satisfy the schema specifications are discarded and the errors tracked.In case of valid datasets, a sequence of preprocessing operations are used. Duplicate records are detected and deleted giving no redundancy. The predefined imputation strategies are used to fill in missing values in order to retain the completeness of the data sets. In addition, categorical variables are encoded in the same way in order to ensure uniformity in the data sets.In order to deal with semantic heterogeneity, disease names in Dnew are standardized through controlled vocabulary or ontology mapping approach. This stage will provide consistency in the disease entities of various data sources.After the preprocessing and standardization, the cleaned data is combined with an existing master data (Dmaster). The combined output is the final cleaned data (Dclean), and this is stored in long term storage to be analysed downstream. A snapshot of the processed data at the time of processing is also archived to facilitate reproducibility and version control.The resulting dataset (Dclean) is a quality and standardized input of the further analytical elements, such as risk assessment and decision-support models of the proposed framework.3.5.2Risk evaluation agent and deterministic risk assessment(a) Risk Evaluation and Deterministic Rule-Based Scoring: The TransmiRisk-AI is a framework that uses a rule-based scoring procedure with a deterministic approach to characterize the baseline zoonotic transmission risk of specific epidemiological attributes. The aim of this component is to deliver a clear, reproducible evaluation which can be used consistently across diseases. The system automatically computes a score based on predefined attributes of a disease using a scoring function implemented in Python, instead of assigning them manually to each disease.The five main dimensions are taken into account: type of transmission, involvement of animals, length and contagiousness of the disease, high risk groups of people and environmental context. The contribution of each dimension is determined using predefined rules. The following factors will contribute to up to 3 points: transmission characteristics, animal involvement, duration and contagious period, high-risk human groups, and environmental context will contribute up to 1.5 points each. The maximum number of points is then 10. The calculation of the risk score is presented in Equation 1.RSi=Ti+Ai+Di+Hi+Ei(1)where RSi is the rule-based score for disease i, Ti represents the transmission type, Ai represents animal involvement, Di represents disease duration and contagious period, Hi represents high-risk human groups, and Ei represents the environmental context. Table 2 provides Deterministic rule-based scoring criteria implemented in TransmiRisk-AI A numerical score is derived and then fixed thresholds are used to categorize the risk into three levels. The rule-based scores for each disease are also categorized as Low Risk (diseases with scores lower than 4), Moderate Risk (diseases with scores between 4 and less than 7), and High Risk (diseases with scores 7 or higher). The risk-level classification is defined in Equation 2.RiskLeveli={Low,RSi<4,Moderate,4≤RSi<7,High,RSi≥7.(2)Table 2Rule-based risk dimensions and scoring criteria.Risk dimensionConditionScoreTransmission typeDirect, airborne, or respiratory transmission3.0Vector-borne, mosquito-, tick-, or flea-associated transmission2.0Other/indirect transmission1.0Animal involvementLivestock, cattle, or poultry2.0Dogs or cats1.5Wildlife, bats, or rodents1.0Duration/contagious periodChronic, months, or weeks2.0Days1.0High-risk human groupsImmunocompromised, pregnant, elderly, or healthcare workers1.5Children1.0Environmental contextRural, farm, or market environments1.5Urban or indoor environments1.0Maximum possible score 10.0 The bold value indicates the maximum possible score of the risk-scoring framework.(b) Integrating Spillover Score: An independent ecological risk component was added complementing the rule-based assessment, based on pathogen-level scores from the SpillOver database. SpillOver ranks zoonotic viruses according to the characteristics of both virus and host. The SpillOver data were imported into the model as a new dataset and standardized prior to being integrated with the TransmiRisk data.The disease and pathogen names were standardized as lowercase text and without leading/trailing space to establish a correspondence between the two datasets. The only records that were kept were those of zoonotic viruses in the SpillOver dataset. Finally, The original SpillOver ranking was then incorporated into the integrated dataset. Because the original SpillOver values are not necessarily expressed on the same numerical scale as the rule-based score, the values were normalized before integration by using Equation 3.Snorm,i=10×Si−SminSmax−Smin(3)where Si represents the original SpillOver score for pathogen i, and Smin and Smax represent the minimum and maximum SpillOver scores in the matched dataset, respectively. If for a specific disease a matching SpillOver record existed, the original SpillOver Total Score was kept as SpillOver Score. In the current implementation, diseases with no associated SpillOver record were given a value of “0”. The SpillOver score was then scaled to a 0–10 range with the maximum score of SpillOver observed.The SpillOver score is an ecological score that complements the rule-based score used for the transmission. full_text_sections.discussion: 5DiscussionThis study has shown that TransmiRisk-AI offers a viable and scalable solution to real-time surveillance of zoonotic diseases, integrating hybrid risk analytics with an agentic AI architecture. Contrary to the conventional surveillance systems, which work reactively and in a disjointed fashion, the proposed system will provide the opportunity to conduct permanent monitoring, automated decision-making, and prioritization of risks on the fly, eliminating key vulnerabilities in the existing public health infrastructure.5.1Importance of agentic AI in surveillanceThe adoption of the agentic AI paradigm of epidemiological intelligence is one of the main contributions of the work. The multi-agent architecture, which includes data ingestion, risk evaluation, alerting, execution, logging and orchestration agents, allows end-to-end automation of the surveillance pipeline. This design will greatly minimize manual intervention, uniformity in data processing, and prompt identification of the risks that occur. The orchestrator is important in ensuring coordination of workflow and thus the system is both robust towards scheduled and event-driven execution.The fact that the agents are able to act independently and that they are traceable through logging mechanisms also increases efficiency and transparency in operations. This is especially so in health care settings, especially in the public where decisions and accountability are crucial.5.2Adaptation of dynamic risk and real-time responsivenessOne of the advantages of TransmiRisk-AI is its ability to respond to real-time outbreak indicators. The system dynamically re-calibrates risk scores of diseases based on recency, frequency and severity of reported events, by incorporating outbreak intelligence into the risk evaluation pipeline. This allows an adaptive prioritization to happen, in which the diseases could move along risk categories as more data is made available.The fact that the case study analyses, including the risk escalation in Crimean–Congo Hemorrhagic Fever and the risk changes increment in the Nipah virus outbreaks, reflect the ability of the system to capture the temporal dynamics is successful. This dynamic flexibility is a huge improvement on the old-fashioned prioritization systems that are usually not responsive to the fast-changing epidemiological realities.5.3System performance and practical utilityThe experimental analysis shows that the system has an efficient execution with a low processing time and an excellent alert accuracy. The fact that updates can be processed in seconds points out its appropriateness in real-time deployment. Another aspect, the precise determination of high-risk diseases, and the correct detection of the transitions between risk categories confirm the quality of the underlying workflow.In terms of usability, the addition of a dashboard based on Streamlit makes it easier to access by the stakeholders of the public health. The platform can enable informed decision-making without the need to possess advanced technical skills by converting complex analytical results into easily understandable visualizations, like risk categories, outbreak trends, and system logs.5.4Comparison with existing systemsCurrent outbreak intelligence systems are mainly centered around reporting and early warning indicators, in contrast to the built-in risk quantification and automation. On the same note, a lot of AI-based models lack multi-disease prioritization and real-time flexibility, being disease-specific. TransmiRisk-AI overcomes these shortcomings by integrating multi-source data, hybrid risk scores, and agent-based automation in a single framework.Also, whereas in the past, non-explainable and non-transparent systems were common, logging mechanisms and interpretable risk outputs in TransmiRisk-AI raise the level of trust and usability among decision-makers. This makes the system a transition between data-driven analytics and usable intelligence on public health.5.5GeneralizabilityGeneralizability to Other Endemic Diseases: The proposed Agentic AI architecture is an extensible surveillance framework that is not endemic disease specific. The existing TransmiRisk database comprises 124 zoonotic diseases, including the Dengue virus (DENV), which can be evaluated in the existing framework of risk assessment. The modular design of the agent architecture allows the application of the same workflow to other diseases by adding disease-specific epidemiological, ecological, and outbreak information. A possible extension, Chagas disease, will be added when the needed standardized information is available. These extensions will have to be independently validated to ensure that the disease-specific risk characteristics and surveillance signals are represented.5.6LimitationsAlthough it has some strong points, there are a number of limitations to be considered. Real-time data on outbreaks may vary in quality and availability between regions and diseases and determines the efficiency of the system. Late or missing reporting may affect the accuracy of risk estimation. Also, although the agentic architecture offers automation, it is not yet based on adaptive learning or self-optimization, and is instead based on predefined workflows.The ongoing implementation is also not based on the complete integration of other influential factors, such as climate variability, mobility patterns, or genomic data, which are known to influence zoonotic transmission dynamics. The addition of these dimensions may also improve predictive potential and situational awareness.The diagnostic approach is a rule-based assessment that is deterministic and reproducible; however, the scoring criteria and thresholds have been methodological choices that have not been statistically optimized to an independent gold standard outcome. As a result, the categories obtained represent relative risk characterisation levels, not “calibrated” probabilities of zoonosis transmission. Future studies will assess for other weights and thresholds as well as test the framework with independent epidemiological and outbreak data sets.5.7Implications to public healthTransmiRisk-AI has profound implications for contemporary public health surveillance. The system facilitates proactive intervention measures and effective allocation of resources, as it allows the early detection of diseases with high risks and continuous monitoring of risks. The automated alerting system will keep people aware of critical risk signals in real time, minimizing lag in response time.In addition, the framework is aligned with the One Health approach as it helps to integrate different data sources and cross-sectoral collaboration. Its modularity and scalability to regional, national, or global levels make it an option to implement a pathway towards intelligent, data-driven surveillance ecosystems.In general, TransmiRisk-AI is a significant step towards autonomous, explainable, and real-time zoonotic disease monitoring, which is a significant issue in the modern public health system.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 6ConclusionThis article introduces TransmiRisk-AI, an agent-based artificial intelligence system that is intended to be used for real-time surveillance and risk monitoring of zoonotic diseases in an autonomous manner. The proposed system overcomes key shortcomings of conventional surveillance methods such as the absence of automation, slow reaction, and minimal flexibility to changing outbreaks by combining a hybrid risk scoring model with a coordinated multi-agent architecture.The agentic design, consisting of data ingestion, risk evaluation, alerting, execution and orchestration agents, enables the ongoing data processing, dynamic risk recalculation and automated dissemination of alerts in real time. Real-time outbreak intelligence makes the system more responsive to changes in disease risk profiles as new events appear and enable it to detect and reflect them. Moreover, the interactive dashboard allows the intuitively visual representation of risk categories, outbreak trends, and system logs, enhancing situational awareness of the public health stakeholders.Experimental findings show that TransmiRisk-AI is an efficient model in execution time, scalability, and accuracy of alerting, and it can effectively model the outbreak-driven changes in zoonotic risk. The case studies also confirm that the system is able to adjust to real-world epidemiological shifts and offer actionable information to make decisions.Altogether, TransmiRisk-AI adds a scalable, explainable, and autonomous surveillance technology that covers the gap between operational public health intelligence and risk modeling with data. The framework shows how agentic AI can turn traditional surveillance systems into proactive, constantly learning ecosystems to help make timely and informed interventions in zoonotic disease control.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionThe issue of zoonotic diseases is an acute and dynamic challenge to the health of people worldwide, caused by a complicated relationship among human, animal, and environmental systems (1). The growing number of emerging infectious diseases, such as Ebola virus disease, Nipah virus infection, and avian influenza, underscores the importance of having surveillance systems that can quickly identify, evaluate, and counter dynamic transmission threats (2). Traditional surveillance methods, using manual reporting and retrospective analysis, tend to be reactive in nature and are unable to deliver timely and data-driven insights to proactively intervene (3).In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has made it possible to create intelligent surveillance systems with the ability to handle large and heterogeneous volumes of data, such as outbreak reports, environmental data, and epidemiological records (4). Examples of AI-powered tools (event-based surveillance systems, digital disease detection tools) have shown that they can help detect the initial signs of an outbreak and enhance situational awareness. Nevertheless, most of these systems are still constrained by disaggregated data integration, lack of automation, and inability to provide continuous risk assessment and prioritization of various diseases.The major weakness of the current AI-based surveillance systems lies in the fact that they are based on fixed or disease-specific models that fail to dynamically change in response to changing outbreak conditions. Also, the majority of systems are labor-intensive to process and analyze data and make decisions, which makes them less efficient and scalable in practice in the context of public health. The lack of synchronized working procedures and automated pipelines also limit the possibility to convert raw material into an actionable intelligence in real time (5).A promising next-generation form of surveillance is agentic artificial intelligence, where autonomous, goal-oriented systems, sensitive to their environment, perform tasks using coordinated activities. Through the use of multi-agent architectures, agentic AI systems can break down complex workflows into specialized functions including data ingestion, risk computation, alert generation and decision support. Such systems allow uninterrupted surveillance, adaptive learning and automatic response systems, which increases efficiency and responsiveness of surveillance systems (6).Herein, this paper suggests TransmiRisk-AI, an agentic AI-based autonomous surveillance system to monitor the risk of zoonotic diseases in real-time. The suggested system will combine a hybrid risk assessment model with a multi-agent structure comprising data ingestion, risk evaluation, alerting, execution, logging, and orchestration agents. The framework facilitates ongoing data integration, real time recalculation of risks based on real time outbreak intelligence, and automatic alerting of high-risk diseases. An interactive dash-board is created to offer a clear visualisation of the risk categories, outbreak trends, and system operations.The concept of agentic AI is autonomous systems that have the ability to perceive their surroundings and perform actions to meet desired objectives and the form of intelligence that replicates human cognitive processes, including learning and solving problems (7). This idea has become popular because AI technologies, such as intelligent agents, now form part of everyday life, which makes people discuss the legal and moral consequences of AI technologies (8). The development of agentic AI is highly associated with the development of interactive systems especially in the virtual worlds where the agentic AIs can develop and perform in complex situations (9). Moreover, the human-machine relations are becoming more interdependent, with AI systems being created to benefit the decision-making process in many applications. Therefore, agentic AI is an important boundary in the history of technology as well as the history of ethics.There are a number of advantages to taking an agentic approach to artificial intelligence systems, especially in the operational areas of improving autonomy, decision-making, and user trust. Using the natural ability to adapt and optimize within a dynamic environment, AI as agents can perform independent actions to adapt through reinforcement learning which is apparent in multi-agent systems in applications of the IoT (10, 11). This enables proactive behavior and therefore the systems can identify any pattern and assume the needs of the user, which enhances user experience and satisfaction. Moreover, explainable AI (XAI) can be integrated, thereby establishing transparency, enabling users to know the reason AI made this decision, which is essential in establishing trust (12). Moreover, conceptual frameworks describing the idea of artificial agency may facilitate the connection between theory and practice, thus maximizing the usefulness of AI in research and practice settings (13). In general, an agentic approach does not only make the AI systems more functional, but also closer to human-like processes of decision making (14).Now that agentic artificial intelligence systems have the ability to catalog and predict zoonotic disease outbreaks earlier, the source of data available to use to detect and forecast these outbreaks is immense through the use of the large volumes of open-source data and highly developed machine learning algorithms. Such systems, including EPIWATCH and BlueDot, employ artificial algorithms to examine various pieces of information, including social media, news stories, and health records, and therefore spot the possible early signs of an outbreak before conventional health authorities do (15, 16). As an example, EPIWATCH was able to predict the first signs of Mpox outbreaks by tracking reports of rash and fever cases, which proves its ability to issue the necessary warnings in time (16). Moreover, it is possible to use AI models to synthesize complex epidemiological data, which makes them useful in timely responding and making informed decisions by the officials of the health sector, thereby reducing the effects of any emerging infectious disease (17). AI adoption into surveillance in public health is a revolutionary way of dealing with zoonotic threats, and there is a necessity to expand the usage of such technologies (18).The implementation of the agentic AI in the current zoonotic disease surveillance systems has both huge opportunities and difficulties. On the bright side, AI is able to intensify predictive modelling and recognition of risk factors to zoonotic illnesses to enhance the detection and response measures to outbreaks (17). It is able to process large quantities of data originating in various sources e.g., social media and environmental surveillance enabling real-time situational awareness and epidemiological insights (19, 20). Nevertheless, there are also the challenges of the complex nature of environmentally-driven zoonoses that tend to dodge the conventional surveillance systems and require the more integrated One Health methodology that covers not only human but also animal and environmental health (21). Also, the differences in surveillance capabilities, especially in the developing world, can make the implementation and reporting processes more challenging, which will make the overall effectiveness of AI-enhanced models more complex (22). Therefore, as much as the fusion of AI is promising it deserves attention given to these complex issues.Agentic AI—autonomous, goal-driven systems capable of performing complex workflows—has recently demonstrated significant potential across scientific and industrial domains. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop an AI-based framework for real-time risk assessment of zoonotic diseases, addressing the limitations of conventional surveillance systems that are reactive and lack automation. The background highlights the need for a system that can dynamically update risk profiles based on outbreak conditions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the development and experimental assessment of the TransmiRisk-AI framework, which was tested using case studies of zoonotic diseases. The framework was designed to integrate outbreak intelligence and provide continuous risk assessment.
analysis.methods: The framework uses a structured dataset for zoonotic diseases, with outbreak data integrated through a modular architecture. It employs rule-based and SpillOver components for initial risk evaluation and dynamically recalculates risk scores based on outbreak recency, frequency, and severity.
analysis.main_results: The framework demonstrated the ability to dynamically recalibrate risk scores using outbreak intelligence. For example, the Nipah virus had a composite risk score of 6.39976 without outbreak data, which increased to 6.50776 after incorporating an outbreak score of 0.54, resulting in a reclassification to high risk.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the agentic AI design enables continuous risk assessment and automated decision-making, which is a novel approach compared to conventional systems. The framework's ability to adapt to changing outbreak conditions is a key innovation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that TransmiRisk-AI can improve situational awareness and risk prioritization for zoonotic diseases, particularly Nipah virus, by integrating real-time outbreak data. This has implications for enhancing public health preparedness and response.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to case study examples and does not provide empirical validation of the framework's performance in real-world settings. The evidence is moderate as it is based on simulated scenarios and theoretical design rather than extensive field testing.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces TransmiRisk-AI, an agentic AI framework designed to enhance real-time risk assessment of zoonotic diseases, with a focus on Nipah virus. The framework integrates outbreak intelligence and hybrid risk scoring models to dynamically update disease risk profiles. It uses a structured dataset and rule-based components for initial risk evaluation, with outbreak data improving the composite risk score. The system enables automated decision-making and prioritization, offering a scalable solution to address the limitations of conventional surveillance methods. However, the study is based on case studies and lacks empirical validation, resulting in moderate evidence strength. The framework's ability to adapt to changing outbreak conditions has significant implications for improving public health preparedness and response to zoonotic diseases.

elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,代理人工智能设计可以实现持续的风险评估和自动化决策,与传统系统相比,这是一种新颖的方法。该框架适应不断变化的 暴发 条件的能力是一项关键创新。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,TransmiRisk-AI 可以通过整合实时 暴发 数据来提高人畜共患疾病(特别是 尼帕病毒)的态势感知和风险优先级。这对于加强公共卫生准备和应对具有重要意义。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于案例研究示例,并未提供框架在现实环境中性能的实证验证。证据是温和的,因为它基于模拟场景和理论设计,而不是广泛的现场测试。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop an AI-based framework for real-time risk assessment of zoonotic diseases, addressing the limitations of conventional surveillance systems that are reactive and lack automation. The background highlights the need for a system that can dynamically update risk profiles based on outbreak conditions.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study involved the development and experimental assessment of the TransmiRisk-AI framework, which was tested using case studies of zoonotic diseases. The framework was designed to integrate outbreak intelligence and provide continuous risk assessment.
analysis_en.methods: The framework uses a structured dataset for zoonotic diseases, with outbreak data integrated through a modular architecture. It employs rule-based and SpillOver components for initial risk evaluation and dynamically recalculates risk scores based on outbreak recency, frequency, and severity.
analysis_en.main_results: The framework demonstrated the ability to dynamically recalibrate risk scores using outbreak intelligence. For example, the Nipah virus had a composite risk score of 6.39976 without outbreak data, which increased to 6.50776 after incorporating an outbreak score of 0.54, resulting in a reclassification to high risk.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the agentic AI design enables continuous risk assessment and automated decision-making, which is a novel approach compared to conventional systems. The framework's ability to adapt to changing outbreak conditions is a key innovation.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that TransmiRisk-AI can improve situational awareness and risk prioritization for zoonotic diseases, particularly Nipah virus, by integrating real-time outbreak data. This has implications for enhancing public health preparedness and response.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to case study examples and does not provide empirical validation of the framework's performance in real-world settings. The evidence is moderate as it is based on simulated scenarios and theoretical design rather than extensive field testing.
